Fujimino, Saitama, Japan mo-kurokawa@kddi-research.jp ## ABSTRACT Building high-quality recommender systems is challenging for new services and small companies, because of their sparse interactions. Cross-domain recommendations (CDRs) alleviate this issue by transferring knowledge from data in external domains. However, most existing CDRs leverage data from only a single external domain and serve only two domains. CDRs serving multiple domains require domain-shared entities (i.e., users and items) to transfer knowledge, which significantly limits their applications due to the hardness and privacy concerns of finding such entities. We therefore focus on a more general scenario, non-overlapped multi-target CDRs (NO-MTCDRs), which require no domain-shared entities and serve multiple domains. Existing methods require domain-shared users to learn user preferences and cannot work on NO-MTCDRs. We hence propose MITrans, a novel mutual information-based (MI-based) preference disentangling and transferring framework to improve recommendations for all domains. MITrans effectively leverages knowledge from multiple domains as well as learning both domain-shared and domain-specific preferences without using domain-shared users. In MITrans, we devise two novel MI constraints to disentangle domain-shared and domain-specific preferences. Moreover, we introduce a module that fuses domain-shared preferences in different domains and combines them with domain-specific preferences to improve recommendations. ACM, New York, NY, USA, 10 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3626772.3657780 ## 1 INTRODUCTION Recently, deep learning-based recommendation models have gained wide attention because of their superiority in predicting preferences accurately \( \left\lbrack {{26},{29},{45}}\right\rbrack \) . Due to the data-hungry nature of deep learning, however, learning deep models with insufficient training data results in impaired performances [44, 52]. To address this issue, cross-domain recommendations (CDRs) have been studied. CDRs can be categorized into single-target, dual-target, and multi-target cases [18, 22, 44]. Most existing efforts consider the former two cases. They focus on scenarios with only two domains and improve recommendation performances on the target domain or on the two domains. Single-target CDRs learn and transfer knowledge based on the data from an external source domain to facilitate the recommendations in the sparse target domain [30, 53]. Dual-target CDRs design dual-learning frameworks to improve recommendations in the source and target domains simultaneously [23, 24]. --- *Corresponding author. ---

Some recent efforts consider that user preferences in CDRs consist of domain-shared and domain-specific preferences. Their experimental results demonstrate that transferring the domain-specific preferences leads to a negative transfer issue, i,e., the knowledge transferred from the source domain degrades the recommendation performance in the target domain \( \left\lbrack {{25},{27},{28},{40}}\right\rbrack \) . Some works mitigate the negative transfer issue by learning and transferring domain-shared preferences \( \left\lbrack {5,{22},{32},{39},{46}}\right\rbrack \) . Using domain-shared users, they learn a global representation for each user across all domains by aggregating their interactions in each domain, or they learn local representations for each user in each domain and then align these local representations across different domains. By doing so, the global and aligned local representations can learn and transfer domain-shared preferences. Recent studies introduce individual-level mutual information (MI) and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between user or item representations learned in different domains to extract both domain-specific and domain-shared preferences \( \left\lbrack {6,9}\right\rbrack \) . Given their explicit measurement of domain differences,such MI and KL-divergence methods have empirically shown their superiority in handling the negative transfer issue and improving recommendation performance. Unfortunately, the above methods still have important challenges in practical usage. (i) These works leave a challenge in building recommender systems (RSs) that can serve multiple domains and leveraging knowledge from diverse source domains. This challenge is prevalent across various industries and applications. For example, in e-commerce platforms such as Amazon and eBay, (1) their RSs need to make recommendations for various categories (domains) of products simultaneously, (2) the number of domains is more than two, and (3) exploiting existing single- and dual-target CDRs is not trivial because, to obtain their best performances, we need to test all pairs of domains, which is impractical. (ii) They rely on domain-shared users, so they are unavailable in non-overlapped CDRs, i.e., CDRs with neither domain-shared users nor domain-shared items. The requirement for (many) domain-shared users significantly limits their applications, because we may have technological and legal difficulty in identifying users across domains and, given some domains (of even the same platform, e.g., Amazon), it is not guaranteed that we have a sufficient number of domain-shared users for learning. There exist non-overlapped CDRs \( \left\lbrack {7,{31},{36}}\right\rbrack \) ,and they learn domain-shared preferences through aligning learned user representations, learned item representations, and prediction scores across domains at the distribution level. The existing non-overlapped CDRs assume single-target or dual-target scenarios, and their alignment operation only extracts domain-shared preferences or even learns a preference containing strong bias towards domains with dense and rich interaction data. They hence cannot work on multi-target scenarios and produce impaired recommendations due to ignore domain-specific preferences. Also, some works developed multi-target CDRs [5, 22], but they require domain-shared users to transfer individual knowledge. To overcome the above limitations and challenges, we consider a non-overlapped multi-target CDR, which is a general setting because it does not limit the number of domains and does not require domain-shared users (items). To this end, we propose MITrans, a novel MI-based preference disentangling and transferring framework. Inspired by the CLUB [8] upper bound for MI, we propose a novel anchor-free variant of CLUB, AFCLUB, to measure the MI between the item representations in different domains. The domain-shared preferences can be learned by minimizing AFCLUB, and, different from CLUB, AFCLUB removes the requirement for domain-shared users and items by estimating the MI for all pairs of items from different domains. Moreover, we develop a novel anchor-free domain-contrastive estimation, AFDCE, to serve as a lower bound for the MI between the item representations in different domains, and we maximize AFDCE to learn domain-shared preferences. By measuring the similarities between all pairs of items from the same and different domains, AFDCE removes the requirement for domain-shared users and items and can serve the non-overlapped scenario. We further develop a multi-domain graph transfer to transfer and fuse the learned domain-shared preferences among multiple domains. After that, we combine the domain-shared preferences with the domain-specific preferences in each domain to improve the recommendations in all domains simultaneously. A summary of our contributions is as follows: - We consider the scenario of non-overlapped multi-target CDRs, which is a ubiquitous scenario in real-world recommendations but has not been studied yet. To study this scenario, we propose MITrans, a novel MI-based preference disentangling and transferring framework. - In MITrans, we introduce a novel upper bound (AFCLUB) and a novel lower bound (AFDCE) for MI to explicitly measure the MI between user preferences in different domains. Thanks to these new techniques, MITrans can learn both domain-specific and domain-shared preferences without requiring domain-shared users and items. - We conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets to show the superiority of MITrans on multi-target CDRs both with and without domain-shared users. Our source code of MITrans is available at https://github.com/ZL6298/MITrans. ## 2 RELATED WORK Preference-disentangled CDR. DAL (Domain Adversarial Learning) [13] and RSA (Representation Space Alignment) are two mainstream technologies for learning domain-shared preferences. Conventional DAL-based studies construct a domain discriminator to force the feature extractor generating domain-invariant representations for users. DARec [43] constrains the domain-invariant quality of user preferences by maximizing the cross-entropy between the domain labels predicted by the domain discriminator and the ground truth labels, and it measures the individual cross-entropy over domain-shared users. \( {\mathrm{C}}^{2}\mathrm{{DSR}} \) [4] captures domain-invariant preferences by fusing users' source and target interactions and maximizing ML between single- and cross-domain user preferences. RecSys-DAN [36], DPMCDR [12], and TDAR [42] remove the requirement for domain-shared users. They capture domain-invariant preferences by measuring the cross-entropy between all source and target users or model a consistent latent preference distribution shared among source and target users, while TDAR requires user review data to learn representations for users and items. RSA-based methods align learned user representations, learned item representations, and predictions across domains to capture domain-shared preferences. For example, COAST [47] and HGCN [14] propose graph-based approaches to align and combine user representations across domains. To benefit recommendations with both domain-shared and domain-specific preferences, SER [9] and DisenCDR [6] introduced ML and KL-divergence to measure the difference between the user representations learned in different domains. However, the aforementioned methods measure differences or learn representations over domain-shared users, so they cannot work on non-overlapped scenarios. Some works remove this requirement by aligning the representation space in a distribution manner. As an instance, CDR-MMT [21] developed regularization to implicitly punish the difference between the contextual features learned in different domains. ESAM [7] aligns the attribution correlation for the learned user representations between source and target domains. CAFF [31] further improves ESAM by adding another distribution alignment constraint. SRTrans [28] developed a task-oriented knowledge distillation approach to capture domain-shared preferences. These previous non-overlapped CDRs lack explicit mechanisms that extract domain-specific preferences, so extending them to the multi-target scenario is difficult.

Multi-target CDRs. Multi-target CDRs have emerged to improve the recommendation performances for multiple domains simultaneously by combining the knowledge in different domains. For example, GA-MTCDR [21] developed a feature combination layer to combine the interaction graph and item similarity information in each domain. HeroGRAPH [10] aggregates the interaction graph of all domains via domain-shared users and constructs a heterogeneous graph to combine the knowledge from each domain. MPF [41], UniCDR [5], and CAT-ART [22] collect each user's interaction data in all domains and learn both global and local user representations. Specifically, CAT-ART and MPF combine global and local user representations to capture domain-shared and domain-specific preferences, while UniCDR aligns these two types of representations to learn a robust domain-shared preference and ignores the domain-specific preferences. These multi-target methods transfer individual knowledge across domains via domain-shared users, so they are unavailable in the non-overlapped scenario. ## 3 PROBLEM STATEMENT Given a set of domains \( \mathcal{D} = \left\{ {{\mathcal{D}}^{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{D}}^{{N}_{d}}}\right\} \) ,the recommendation task of multi-target CDRs in this work is the top-K recommendation in all domains,where \( {N}_{d} \) denotes the number of domains. Let \( {\mathcal{U}}^{d} \) and \( {\mathcal{V}}^{d} \) respectively denote sets of users and items in \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) . The interaction set between \( {\mathcal{U}}^{d} \) and \( {\mathcal{V}}^{d} \) is denoted as \( {\mathcal{R}}^{d} = \{ \left( {u,v}\right) \mid u \in \; \left. {{\mathcal{U}}^{d},v \in {\mathcal{V}}^{d}}\right\} \) . Under the scenario of non-overlapped CDRs,there is no overlap of user and item between any domains. In each domain \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) ,the top-K recommendation aims to generate personalized rankings from candidate items \( {\overline{\mathcal{V}}}_{u}^{d} \) and recommends the top-K items for each user \( u \) in \( {\mathcal{U}}^{d} \) ,where \( {\overline{\mathcal{V}}}_{u}^{d} \) is an item set containing items with no interaction with \( u \) . To achieve this,we introduce a prediction model \( f\left( {u,v}\right) \) ,which, given a user \( u \) and an item \( v \) ,predicts a preference score \( {y}_{u,v} = \; f\left( {u,v}\right) \) . Then,for each user \( u \) ,the candidate items can be ordered based on their preference scores \( {}^{1} \) . The main notations are summarised in Table 1. Table 1: Summary of notations

## 4 MITRANS Previous CDRs either lack explicit mechanisms that capture both domain-specific and domain-shared preferences or require domain-shared users to transfer knowledge across domains. We remove these limitations and, for non-overlapped multi-target CDRs, propose MITrans, an MI-based preference disentangling and transferring framework. Its overview is shown in Figure 1. MITrans consists of three modules. The numbers below correspond to the modules in Figure 1. (1) The semantic embedding module extracts semantic embeddings for items from their text data. These embeddings are leveraged to (i) capture domain-specific and domain-shared preferences in the second module and (ii) construct cross-domain graphs that transfer knowledge across multiple domains. (2) In the disentangled preference learning module, we develop domain-shared and domain-specific encoders, which respectively generate domain-shared and domain-specific embeddings for items by inputting the semantic embeddings extracted in the semantic embedding module. We then propose two novel MI-based constraints to disentangle domain-shared and domain-specific preferences from the two types of item embeddings. (3) In the preference fusing module, we adaptively cluster items with their semantic embeddings and construct two types of cross-domain graphs. The adjacency matrices of these graphs are defined as the cosine similarities between semantic embeddings of items and item clusters in different domains. Then, we aggregate the structural information in these graphs to enhance the domain-shared item em-beddings in each domain. By doing so, domain-shared preferences in diverse domains can be fused into each domain without requiring domain-shared users and items. After that, we combine these enhanced domain-shared preferences with the domain-specific preferences to further improve recommendation performances. ### 4.1 Semantic Embedding Module Previous studies have empirically shown that semantic embeddings of items are effective in transferring knowledge between domains with homogeneous or heterogeneity user behaviors \( \left\lbrack {{27},{28},{37},{38}}\right\rbrack \) . --- \( {}^{1} \) Any search algorithms which allow arbitrary user and item embeddings (e.g.,[1- 3, 16, 33]) are available. ---

Figure 1: Overview of MITrans Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) are expected to provide robust token representations containing semantic information [48]. To obtain semantic item embeddings, we employ a prevailing LLM, i.e., BERT[11], and extract token embeddings for each token in the text data of items (item descriptions in this work). Formally, given an item \( v \) ,we denote its text and semantic embedding as \( \operatorname{text}\left( v\right) \) and \( \mathbf{v} \) ,respectively,and \( \mathbf{v} \) is formulated as: \[\mathbf{v} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{t \in \operatorname{text}\left( v\right) }}{\phi }_{\mathrm{{tf}} - \mathrm{{idf}}}\left( t\right) \cdot {\phi }_{\mathrm{{BERT}}}\left( t\right) , \tag{1}\] where \( {\phi }_{\text{ tf-idf }}\left( t\right) \) is the tf-idf score calculated with the corpus containing the text data of all items in a domain. We weight tokens based on their tf-idf scores to mitigate the impact of tokens that lack meaning but are frequently present. To preserve user privacy and increase the applicability of our method, we apply traditional ID embedding for users. For each domain \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) ,the embedding for user \( u \in {\mathcal{U}}^{d} \) is defined as a trainable vector \( \mathbf{u} \) ,which \( u \) ’s ID can retrieve. Then,the user embeddings in \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) are denoted as an embedding matrix \( {\mathbf{U}}^{d} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{\left| {\mathcal{U}}_{d}\right| \times {N}_{e}} \) ,where \( \left| {\mathcal{U}}_{d}\right| \) is the number of users in \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) while \( {N}_{e} \) is the number of embedding dimensions. Each row in \( {\mathbf{U}}^{d} \) corresponds to a user embedding. ### 4.2 Disentangled Preference Learning Module We propose two MI-based constraints to disentangle domain-shared and domain-specific user preferences. We first introduce a domain-shared encoder and a set of domain-specific encoders to encode semantic item embeddings and generate domain-specific and domain-shared item embeddings. The MI of these two types of embeddings is then measured to optimize these encoders. The optimized encoders are expected to generate embeddings containing domain-shared and domain-specific preferences. Using these preferences has been empirically proven to be superior in alleviating the negative transfer issue and improving recommendations \( \left\lbrack {6,9,{28}}\right\rbrack \) . After that,we employ LGC layers [15] to aggregate multi-hop interaction information into the domain-specific and domain-shared embeddings. The interaction information is obtained from the interaction graph of each domain. Because no additional parameter is introduced, LGC layers have been proven effective in alleviating the over-fitting issue for sparse domains [28]. Finally, our MI-based constraints are leveraged to disentangle domain-specific and domain-shared preferences based on the two types of item embeddings generated by the two types of encoders. 4.2.1 Domain-specific Preference Learning. We first introduce a domain-specific encoder for each domain to create domain-specific item embeddings from their semantic embeddings. Taking domain \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) as an example,we denote the domain-specific encoder and the domain-specific item embeddings in this domain as \( {\phi }^{d} \) and \( {\mathrm{E}}^{d} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{\left| {\mathcal{V}}_{d}\right| \times {N}_{e}} \) ,respectively. Each row in \( {\mathrm{E}}^{d} \) is a domain-specific item embedding. For example,the \( i \) -th row in \( {\mathrm{E}}^{d} \) is the domain-specific embedding \( {\mathbf{e}}_{i}^{d} \) for item \( {v}_{i} \) ,which is \[{\mathbf{e}}_{i}^{d} = {\phi }^{d}\left( {\mathbf{v}}_{i}\right) \tag{2}\] where \( {\mathbf{v}}_{i} \) is the semantic embedding for item \( {v}_{i} \) . Then,the user embedding matrix \( {\mathbf{U}}^{d} \) and the item embedding matrix \( {\mathrm{E}}^{d} \) are inputted into LGC layers to aggregate multi-hop interaction information with the interaction graph \( {\mathrm{G}}^{d}\left( {{\mathrm{U}}^{d},{\mathrm{V}}^{d};{\mathcal{R}}^{d}}\right) \) . In this graph,the vertices correspond to all users and items in domain \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) ,and the edges are the interactions in \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) . The graph convolutional process on \( {\mathrm{G}}^{d} \) is formulated as \[\left( {{\overline{\mathrm{U}}}^{d},{\mathrm{D}}^{d}}\right) = \operatorname{LGC}\left( {{\mathrm{U}}^{d},{\mathrm{E}}^{d} \mid {\mathrm{G}}^{d}\left( {{\mathrm{U}}^{d},{\mathrm{\;V}}^{d};{\mathcal{R}}^{d}}\right) }\right) , \tag{3}\] where \( {\overline{\mathrm{U}}}^{d} \) and \( {\mathrm{D}}^{d} \) are respectively the domain-specific user and item embeddings after aggregation of the interaction information from \( {\mathrm{G}}^{d} \) . By minimizing the mutual information of domain-specific item embeddings across domains, we can learn the domain-specific item embeddings containing domain-specific preferences. CLUB [8] is an approximate upper bound of the MI. It is differentiable and hence can be minimized with the gradient descent algorithm. However, CLUB works only on domain-shared users and items because it estimates the MI between two representations of the same object, e.g., two types of embeddings for a user or an item. This is hence not available in non-overlapped CDRs, so we propose AFCLUB, a novel anchor-free variant of CLUB. AFCLUB measures the mutual information for all item pairs in different domains to remove the identification of domain-shared items, and the AFCLUB between \( {\mathcal{D}}^{m} \) and \( {\mathcal{D}}^{n} \) is formulated as

\[{\mathcal{L}}_{AC}^{m,n} = \frac{1}{{N}_{m}{N}_{m}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{N}_{m}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1,j \neq i}}^{{N}_{m}}\left( {\log p\left( {{\mathbf{d}}_{j}^{m} \mid {\mathbf{d}}_{i}^{m}}\right) - \frac{1}{{N}_{n}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{{N}_{n}}\log p\left( {{\mathbf{d}}_{k}^{n} \mid {\mathbf{d}}_{i}^{m}}\right) }\right) ,\] (4) where \( {\mathbf{d}}_{i}^{m} \) is the \( i \) -th row in \( {\mathbf{D}}^{m} \) ,whereas \( {N}_{m} \) and \( {N}_{n} \) are the numbers of items in \( {\mathcal{D}}^{m} \) and \( {\mathcal{D}}^{n} \) ,respectively. As with \( \left\lbrack {8,{19}}\right\rbrack \) ,we assume that the distribution of the conditional probability \( p\left( {{\mathbf{d}}_{j} \mid {\mathbf{d}}_{i}}\right) \) follows the normal distribution \( \mathcal{N}\left( {{\mathbf{\mu }}_{i},{\mathbf{\sigma }}_{i}^{2}}\right) \) . The conditional probability \( p\left( {{\mathbf{d}}_{j} \mid {\mathbf{d}}_{i}}\right) \) represents the probability that the domain-specific embedding after aggregating \( {\mathrm{G}}^{d} \) for item \( j \) is \( {\mathbf{d}}_{j} \) after observing \( {\mathbf{d}}_{i} \) . When item \( i \) and item \( j \) are from different domains,minimizing \( p\left( {{\mathbf{d}}_{j} \mid {\mathbf{d}}_{i}}\right) \) can mitigate the mutual dependence between \( {\mathbf{d}}_{i} \) and \( {\mathbf{d}}_{j} \) to extract domain-shared features. We design two domain-shared agent networks \( {\phi }_{\mu } \) and \( {\phi }_{\sigma } \) to calculate \( {\mathbf{\mu }}_{i} \) and \( \log {\mathbf{\sigma }}_{i} \) : \[{\mathbf{\mu }}_{\mathbf{i}} = {\phi }_{\mu }\left( {\mathbf{d}}_{\mathbf{i}}\right) ,\;\log {\mathbf{\sigma }}_{\mathbf{i}} = {\phi }_{\sigma }\left( {\mathbf{d}}_{\mathbf{i}}\right) . \tag{5}\] Then, \( p\left( {{\mathrm{\;d}}_{j} \mid {\mathrm{d}}_{i}}\right) \) can be computed by \[p\left( {{\mathbf{d}}_{j} \mid {\mathbf{d}}_{i}}\right) = - \frac{{\left( {\mathbf{\mu }}_{i} - {\mathbf{d}}_{j}\right) }^{2}}{2 \cdot \exp \left( {\log {\mathbf{\sigma }}_{i}}\right) }. \tag{6}\] 4.2.2 Domain-shared Preference Learning. The goal of this part is to learn domain-shared preferences. To achieve this, we first develop a domain-shared encoder \( {\phi }_{s} \) to encode semantic item embeddings. Given a domain \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) ,we denote domain-shared item embeddings in \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) as a matrix \( {\mathbf{H}}^{d} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{\left| {\mathcal{V}}_{d}\right| \times {N}_{e}} \) . Then,the domain-shared embedding for an item \( {v}_{i} \in {\mathcal{V}}^{d} \) is computed as \[{\mathbf{h}}_{i}^{d} = {\phi }^{s}\left( {\mathbf{v}}_{i}\right) \tag{7}\] where \( {\mathbf{v}}_{i} \) is the semantic embedding of item \( {v}_{i} \) . It is important to notice that the encoder \( {\phi }^{s} \) is shared for all domains. After getting \( {\mathrm{H}}^{d} \) ,we input \( {\mathrm{H}}^{d} \) and the user embedding matrix \( {\mathrm{U}}^{d} \) into LGC layers to convolute multi-hop interaction information, that is, \[\left( {{\widehat{\mathbf{U}}}^{d},{\mathrm{\;S}}^{d}}\right) = \operatorname{LGC}\left( {{\mathbf{U}}^{d},{\mathrm{H}}^{d} \mid {\mathrm{G}}^{d}\left( {{\mathbf{U}}^{d},{\mathbf{V}}^{d};{\mathcal{R}}^{d}}\right) }\right) , \tag{8}\] where \( {\widehat{\mathbf{U}}}^{d} \) and \( {\mathbf{S}}^{d} \) are respectively domain-shared user and item embeddings after aggregating interaction information in \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) . Then, we learn domain-shared item embeddings containing domain-shared preferences by maximizing the mutual information between these embeddings in different domains. Information noise contrastive estimation (InfoNCE) is a widely used lower bound that estimates the mutual information between two variables [34]. However, the measurement of InfoNCE demands domain-shared users or items as the anchors in CDRs. Therefore, we propose a novel anchor-free domain contrastive estimation (AFDCE) which can measure the mutual information of the domain-shared item embeddings across domains without using domain-shared users. The inverse AFDCE loss between domain \( {\mathrm{D}}^{m} \) and \( {\mathrm{D}}^{n} \) is defined as: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{iDCE}^{m,n} = - \frac{1}{{N}_{m}{N}_{n}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{N}_{m}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{{N}_{n}}\log \frac{\exp \left( {\cos \left( {{\mathbf{s}}_{i}^{m},{\mathbf{s}}_{j}^{n}}\right) /\tau }\right) }{\frac{1}{{N}_{m}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1,k \neq i}}^{{N}_{m}}\exp \left( {\cos \left( {{\mathbf{s}}_{i}^{m},{\mathbf{s}}_{k}^{m}}\right) /\tau }\right) },\] (9)where \( \cos \left( \cdot \right) \) denotes the cosine similarity function and the hyper-parameter \( \tau \) controls the temperature. By minimizing \( {\mathcal{L}}_{iDCE}^{m,n} \) ,we can maximize the AFDCE lower bound and also maximize the mutual information between domain-shared item embeddings \( {\mathrm{S}}^{m} \) and \( {\mathrm{S}}^{n} \) to capture domain-shared preferences. ### 4.3 Preference Fusing Module This module fuses domain-shared preferences in multiple domains and combines the fused domain-shared preferences and the domain-specific preferences to improve recommendation performances. It consists of a multi-domain graph transfer and a task-oriented preference fusion. 4.3.1 Multi-domain Graph Transfer. To transfer and fuse domain-shared preferences across multi-domains, we develop a multi-domain variant of the two-tier graph transfer in SRTrans [28]. We first adaptively cluster the items in each domain by using their semantic embeddings and compute a cluster embedding for each cluster. Following the idea in DE-RRD [17] and SRTrans [28], we apply a cluster indicator net \( {\phi }_{ci} \) and the widely used Gumbel-Softmax reparame-terization trick to achieve the end-to-end cluster. For each domain \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \in \mathcal{D} \) ,we compute a cluster assignment matrix \( {\mathbf{P}}^{d} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{\left| {\mathcal{V}}^{d}\right| \times {N}_{c}} \) , where the \( i \) -th row of the \( j \) -th column in \( {\mathbf{P}}^{d} \) indicates the probability that item \( {v}_{i} \) is assigned to the cluster \( {c}_{j} \) . Note that \( {N}_{c} \) is the number of clusters. Taking the item \( {v}_{i} \) as an example,the cluster assignment vector of \( {v}_{i} \) is formulated by \[{\mathbf{p}}_{i}^{d} = {\phi }_{ci}\left( {\mathbf{v}}_{i}\right) \tag{10}\] Let \( {\mathbf{M}}^{d} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{\left| {\mathcal{V}}^{d}\right| \times {N}_{c}} \) denote the binary gradient matrix for domain \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) . The \( i \) -th row in \( {\mathbf{M}}^{d} \) indicates the cluster assignment result for item \( {v}_{i} \) and is denoted as \( {\mathbf{m}}_{i}^{d} \) . By using the Gumbel-Softmax reparameterizaztion trick, \( {\mathbf{m}}_{i}^{d} \) can be calculated as \[{\mathbf{m}}_{i}^{d} = \operatorname{Softmax}\left( \frac{{\mathbf{p}}_{i}^{d} + \mathbf{g}}{\tau }\right) ,\;\mathbf{g} \sim \operatorname{Gumbel}\left( {0,1}\right) \tag{11}\] where \( \mathbf{g} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{N}}_{c}} \) is a Gumbel noise drawn from the Gumbel \( \left( {0,1}\right) \) distribution and \( \tau \) is a temperature parameter. After getting \( {\mathbf{M}}^{d} \) ,we denote the cluster matrix in \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) as the average semantic embed-dings of the items assigned to the corresponding clusters: \[{\mathbf{C}}^{d} = {\left( \frac{{\mathbf{M}}^{d}}{\mathop{\sum }\limits_{k}{\mathbf{M}}_{\left\lbrack : ,k\right\rbrack }^{d}}\right) }^{T}{\mathbf{v}}^{d} \tag{12}\] After computing the cluster matrix for all domains, we construct a cluster-level cross-domain graph \( {\mathrm{G}}_{c}\left( {\mathrm{C};\mathcal{A}}\right) \) to aggregate the cluster-level domain-shared preferences in diverse domains ( \( \mathcal{A} \) is shown later). The vertices in \( {\mathrm{G}}_{c} \) contain clusters in all domains, which is \( \mathbf{C} = \operatorname{Concat}\left( {{\mathbf{C}}^{1};\ldots ;{\mathbf{C}}^{{N}_{d}}}\right) \) . The edges in \( {\mathrm{G}}_{c} \) and their corresponding weights are determined as the cosine similarity with softmax between vertices. For example,the edge weight \( \mathcal{A}\left( {{\mathbf{c}}_{i},{\mathbf{c}}_{j}}\right) \) between clusters \( {\mathbf{c}}_{i} \) and \( {\mathbf{c}}_{j} \) is measured by \[\mathcal{A}\left( {{\mathbf{c}}_{i},{\mathbf{c}}_{j}}\right) = \operatorname{Softmax}\left( {\cos \left( {{\mathbf{c}}_{i},{\mathbf{c}}_{j}}\right) }\right) . \tag{13}\] Then,the adjacency matrix in \( {\mathrm{G}}_{c} \) is defined as \( \mathcal{A} = \left\{ {\mathcal{A}\left( {{\mathrm{c}}_{i},{\mathrm{c}}_{j}}\right) \mid {\mathrm{c}}_{i} \in }\right. \; \left. {\mathbf{C},{\mathbf{c}}_{j} \in \mathbf{C}}\right\} \) . (Non-zero weight means that there is an edge.) With the graph \( {\mathrm{G}}_{c}\left( {\mathbf{C};\mathcal{A}}\right) \) ,we fuse and transfer relational knowledge across domains by leveraging a graph convolutional network (GCN) [20], which is formulated as

\[\widehat{\mathbf{C}} = \operatorname{ReLU}\left( {{\widetilde{\mathbf{D}}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}{\widetilde{\mathbf{D}}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{C}{\mathbf{W}}_{c}}\right) . \tag{14}\] In this formula, \( \widetilde{\mathcal{A}} \) is the adjacency matrix after adding self-loops. Also, \( {\mathbf{W}}_{c} \) is the trainable weight matrix in this GCN,and \( \widetilde{\mathbf{D}} \) is the degree matrix with elements \( {\widetilde{D}}_{ii} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{\widetilde{A}}_{ij} \) . Because the cluster embeddings \( \mathbf{C} \) are calculated with domain-shared item embeddings, the GCN is expected to aggregate domain-shared preferences in different domains into the enhanced cluster embeddings \( \widehat{\mathbf{C}} \) . After aggregating the domain-shared preferences into \( \widehat{\mathbf{C}} \) ,we further construct a cluster-item graph for each domain \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \in \mathcal{D} \) to aggregate the domain-shared preferences into the domain-shared item embeddings in that domain. Taking domain \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) as an instance,we denote the cluster-item graph for \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) as \( {\mathrm{G}}_{v}^{d}\left( {{\mathrm{Q}}^{d};{\mathcal{B}}^{d}}\right) \) . Its vertices consist of the clusters in all domains and the items in \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) ,i.e., \( {\mathrm{Q}}^{d} = \operatorname{Concat}\left( {\widehat{\mathrm{C}};{\mathrm{S}}^{d}}\right) \) . Its adjacency matrix is defined as the cosine similarities with softmax between vertices, which is \( {\mathcal{B}}^{d} = \left\{ {{\mathcal{B}}^{d}\left( {{q}_{i},{q}_{j}}\right) \mid {q}_{i},{q}_{j} \in {\mathbf{Q}}^{d}}\right\} \) . With this graph,we next use a GCN to transfer the aggregated knowledge from the cluster em-beddings \( \widehat{\mathbf{C}} \) to the domain-shared item embeddings \( {\mathbf{S}}^{d} \) ,which is formulated as \[{\widehat{\mathrm{Q}}}^{d} = \operatorname{ReLU}\left( {{\widetilde{\mathrm{D}}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}{\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}}^{d}{\widetilde{\mathrm{D}}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}{\mathrm{Q}}^{d}{\mathrm{\;W}}_{v}^{d}}\right) , \tag{15}\] where \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}}^{d} \) is the adjacency matrix with self-loops and \( \widetilde{\mathbf{D}} \) is the degree matrix on \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}}^{d} \) . Also, \( {\mathbf{W}}_{v}^{d} \) is the trainable weight matrix in this GCN. Then,we obtain the enhanced domain-shared item embeddings \( {\widehat{\mathbf{S}}}^{d} \) , containing aggregated domain-shared preferences from multiple domains,as the last \( \left| {\mathcal{V}}^{d}\right| \) rows of \( {\widehat{\mathbf{Q}}}^{d} \) . 4.3.2 Task-oriented Preference Fusion. We achieve preference fusion by distilling domain-shared preferences from the enhanced item embeddings \( {\widehat{\mathrm{S}}}^{d} \) into the domain-specific item embeddings \( {\mathrm{D}}^{d} \) for each domain \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \in \mathcal{D} \) . We compute two types of preference scores with the domain-specific user embeddings \( {\overline{\mathbf{U}}}^{d} \) and the two types of item embeddings \( {\widehat{\mathbf{S}}}^{d} \) and \( {\mathbf{D}}^{d} \) . For simplicity,we explain the computation with the example of an interaction \( \left( {{u}_{i},{v}_{j}}\right) \) . Formally, the two types of preference scores are given by the inner product between the user embedding and the corresponding item embedding: \[{\widehat{y}}_{i,j}^{d} = f\left( {{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_{i}^{d},{\mathbf{d}}_{j}^{d}}\right) \;\text{ and }\;{\widetilde{y}}_{i,j}^{d} = f\left( {{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_{i}^{d},{\widehat{\mathbf{s}}}_{j}^{d}}\right) . \tag{16}\] Then, the preference fusion loss is defined as the KL-divergence between the two types of preference scores, which is \[{\mathcal{L}}_{PF}^{d} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\left( {{u}_{i},{v}_{j}}\right) \in {\mathcal{R}}^{d}}}\left( {{\widehat{y}}_{i,j}^{d}\log \frac{{\widehat{y}}_{i,j}^{d}}{{\widetilde{y}}_{i,j}^{d}} + \left( {1 - {\widehat{y}}_{i,j}^{d}}\right) \log \frac{\left( 1 - {\widehat{y}}_{i,j}^{d}\right) }{\left( 1 - {\widetilde{y}}_{i,j}^{d}\right) }}\right) . \tag{17}\] After minimizing \( {\mathcal{L}}_{PF}^{d} \) ,the domain-shared preferences and the domain-specific preferences can be fused into the domain-specific item embeddings. ### 4.4 Learning Objective We employ the BPR [35] loss to measure the performance of predictions. For our multi-target CDR, the prediction objective is to simultaneously minimize the BPR loss in all domains. For each domain \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \in \mathcal{D} \) ,we extend its interaction set to \( {\mathcal{R}}^{d} = \left\{ {\left( {{u}_{i},{v}_{j},{v}_{k}}\right) \mid {u}_{i} \in {\mathcal{U}}^{d},{v}_{j} \in {\mathcal{V}}^{d},{v}_{k} \in {\overline{\mathcal{V}}}_{u}^{d}}\right\} \) by randomly sampling a negative item \( {v}_{k} \) for each interaction \( \left( {{u}_{i},{v}_{j}}\right) \) . Then,the BPR loss of \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) is measured by \[{\mathcal{L}}_{BPR}^{d} = - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\left( {{u}_{i},{v}_{j},{v}_{k}}\right) \in {\mathcal{R}}^{d}}}\ln \sigma \left( {{\widehat{y}}_{i,j}^{d} - {\widehat{y}}_{i,k}^{d}}\right) , \tag{18}\] where \( \ln \sigma \) is the logistic sigmoid function. Finally,the total loss of MITrans is defined as \[\mathcal{L} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m = 1}}^{{N}_{d}}\left( {{\mathcal{L}}_{BPR}^{m} + \alpha {\mathcal{L}}_{PF}^{m} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{n = 1,n \neq m}}^{{N}_{d}}\left( {\beta {\mathcal{L}}_{AC}^{m,n} + \gamma {\mathcal{L}}_{iDCE}^{m,n}}\right) }\right) , \tag{19}\] where \( \alpha ,\beta \) ,and \( \gamma \) are hyper-parameters that control the weights of each component. In \( \mathcal{L} \) ,minimizing the inverse AFDCE loss \( {\mathcal{L}}_{iDCE}^{m,n} \) and the AFCLUB loss \( {\mathcal{L}}_{AC}^{m,n} \) is expected to disentangle the domain-shared and domain-specific preferences. Then, these preferences are combined into domain-specific item embeddings by minimizing the preference fusion loss \( {\mathcal{L}}_{PF}^{m} \) . ## 5 EXPERIMENT ### 5.1 Datasets Amazon dataset \( {}^{2} \) and Douban dataset \( {}^{3} \) are two widely used benchmarks for CDR evaluation [49-51]. Considering the non-overlapped multi-target CDR task in this work, we selected 4 categories of rating data from Amazon dataset, including Books, Movies and TV (Movies), Sports and Outdoors (Sports), and Video Games (Games), as different domains. We also selected 3 categories of rating data from Douban dataset, including Books, Movies, and Musics, as different domains. Table 2 reports the statistical information of these datasets. 5.1.1 Amazon. For each domain in Amazon, we collected the fivescore ratings on products from 30/6/2017 to 3/10/2018 and descriptions of products in the same period as interaction set and text data of items. In the data pre-processing stage, we first filtered out the interactions for items with no text data. Then, we constructed two CDR scenarios on Amazon dataset, including a sparse scenario and a relatively dense scenario, to evaluate the performance of MITrans in both sparse and dense settings. For the sparse scenario, we sampled 8,000 users with 3 to 5 ratings in each domain to adapt to a sparse setting. On the other hand, for the dense scenario, we sampled 8,000 users with 5 to 15 ratings in each domain to form a relatively dense environment. We also built an overlap scenario on Amazon dataset by identifying domain-shared users in 3 domains, i.e., Books, Movies, and Sports, to compare with CDRs requiring domain-shared users. It is important to note that there is no domain-shared user overlapping in all the 4 domains. 5.1.2 Douban. For each domain in Douban, we collected all ratings with the score larger than 3 and tags of products as interaction set and text data of items. In the data pre-processing stage, we first filtered out the interactions for items with no text data. We sampled items with 5 to 30 ratings in each domain to form a dense environment. --- \( {}^{2} \) jmcauley.ucsd.edu/data/amazon/ \( {}^{3} \) kaggle.com/datasets/fengzhujoey/douban-datasetratingreviewside-information/ ---

### 5.2 Evaluated Method We compared MITrans with the following state-of-the-art methods, including single-domain, non-overlapped, and overlapped CDRs. 5.2.1 Single-domain Methods. We first made comparisons with LightGCN [15], a state-of-the-art graph-based method. LightGCN designs a novel light graph convolutional layer to extract graph knowledge and alleviate the over-fitting issue effectively. 5.2.2 Non-overlapped CDR Methods. In this branch of CDR methods, we compared with RecSys-DAN [36], ESAM [7], and CFAA [31]. These methods capture domain-shared preferences by aligning the distribution of user representations, item representations, or predictions between domains. We also evaluated a recent graph-based CDR method, i.e., SRTrans [28], which learns and transfers relational knowledge between domains to alleviate the negative transfer issue. 5.2.3 Overlapped CDR Methods. COAST [47] and HGCN [14] are state-of-the-art graph-based efforts that learn domain-shared preferences by aligning or fusing user and item preferences between domains. They also construct cross-domain heterogeneous (hyper- )graphs to aggregate high-order graph knowledge. We also compared MITrans with UniCDR [5] and CAT-ART [22], which are state-of-the-art multi-target CDR methods. UniCDR and CAT-ART learn global and local representations for users. The former captures domain-shared preferences by aligning these two types of representations, whereas the latter combines these two representations to capture both domain-shared and domain-specific preferences. ### 5.3 Evaluation Criteria We measured performances of recommendations for all domains. For each user \( u \) in each domain \( {\mathcal{D}}^{d} \) ,we took their last and second-last interactions to serve as the test and the validation data, respectively. The remaining interactions were used as the training data. Then,we randomly selected 99 negative items from \( {\overline{\mathcal{V}}}_{u}^{d} \) and ranked them with the test item based on the calculated preference scores. After that, we recommended the top-K items in the ranking to this user. The performance of the top-K recommendations was measured by the widely used Hit Ratio (HR) and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG). For each domain, we experimented 10 groups of negative items and reported the average performance with the \( {95}\% \) confidence level. We ran experiments for every pair of domains for all single-target and dual-target CDR methods (RecSys-DAN, ESAM, CFAA, SRTrans, COAST, and HGCN). The result on a given dataset is the best performance among all combinations. ### 5.4 Implementation Details The codes of Light \( {\mathrm{{GCN}}}^{4} \) ,UniCDR \( {}^{5} \) ,and CAT-ART \( {}^{6} \) were obtained from the corresponding GitHub repositories. For fair comparisons, we replaced the item embeddings for all evaluated methods with our semantic item embedding that can be calculated by Equation 1. We also unified the base model for all non-overlapped methods as the same LightGCN model. We used the same mini-batch mechanism and Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.01 to train all evaluated methods, where the batch size was 2048. We also set the embedding size \( {N}_{e} \) to 32,64,and 32 for all evaluated methods in the corresponding sparse, dense, and overlapping scenarios. For all non-overlapped methods, the number of LGC layers in the base model was set to 2,3 , and 1 for the sparse, dense, and overlapping scenarios, respectively. The setting of the remaining hyper-parameters in the baselines followed their original papers. In MITrans,we built the two encoders \( {\phi }^{d} \) and \( {\phi }^{s} \) ,the two agent networks \( {\phi }_{\mu } \) and \( {\phi }_{\sigma } \) ,and the cluster indicator net \( {\phi }_{ci} \) as a dense layer with the shape of \( \left\lbrack {{N}_{e},{N}_{e}}\right\rbrack \) . The temperature factor \( \tau \) and the weight of the preference fusion loss \( \alpha \) were 0.0001 and 0.1, respectively. The weight of AFCLUB loss \( \beta \) was 0.01,0.1,and 0 for the experiments in the sparse, dense, and overlapping scenarios, respectively. The weight of AFDCE loss was respectively 0,0.1 , and 0.01 for the corresponding sparse, dense, and overlapping scenarios. These hyper-parameters were set based on the average performance of all domains over the validation set. ### 5.5 Experiment Result 5.5.1 Performance Comparisons. To study the contribution of each module in MITrans, we compared MITrans with its variants, including (1) w/o SE, which removes the semantic embedding module and uses the ID embedding for items, (2) w/o DPL, which removes the AFCLUB and the AFDCE constraints (i.e.,without \( {\mathcal{L}}_{AC} \) and \( {\mathcal{L}}_{iDCE} \) ),and (3) w/o PF, which cuts out the preference fusing module from MITrans. The results on Amazon dataset and Douban dataset are reported respectively in Table 3 and Table 4. From these tables, we find the following observations. (1) All modules contribute to the final preference in most cases. (2) MITrans w/o SE performs the worst. This result shows that semantic feature is essential in improving performance in CDRs, particularly when transferring knowledge based on items. (3) MITrans w/o PF performs better than MITrans in the sparse scenario of Amazon dataset. This variant ignores the domain-shared preferences but improves its performance. This means that the domain-shared preferences degrade the final performance, and this result also explains why non-overlapped baselines, which extract only domain-shared preferences, suffer from the negative transfer issue in the same scenario. 5.5.3 Training Efficiency. This observation indicates that MITrans effectively learns and leverages knowledge from multiple domains to improve its recommendation performance. ## 6 CONCLUSION This work focused on a new CDR task, i.e., non-overlapped multi-target CDR, and proposed MITrans. In MITrans, we extract two types of representations for items from their text data and introduce two novel mutual information-based constraints, i.e., AFCLUB and AFDCE, to learn domain-specific and domain-shared preferences, respectively. Furthermore, we devised a preference fusing module to fuse domain-shared preferences learned in different domains and combine them with domain-specific preferences. We conducted extensive experiments on two real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that MITrans outperforms state-of-the-art non-overlapped CDR methods and achieves at least comparable performances with overlapped CDR methods. Moreover, MITrans empirically shows superiority in leveraging knowledge from multiple domains and alleviating negative transfer. ## ACKNOWLEDGMENTS This work partially supported by JST CREST Grant Number JP-MJCR21F2.
